name: Chloe Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I work as a field researcher for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior cook at Fratelli's, a pizza and pasta place in the retail park off the ring road. Friday nights we do three hundred pizzas, and I'm on the pasta station boiling, saucing and plating, plus dough prep in the mornings. I'm still slow on the dough, the owner's son can stretch a base in ten seconds and I take thirty. But I love it when the whole line is in rhythm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your life like outside the kitchen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Noor, my girlfriend, who's a nursing assistant at the hospital. Money's tight, I've got maybe a week's rent saved, but her job's steady. I use AI every day, honestly, for meal plans, for a little supper club menu I'm dreaming up, even for working out our bills. There's not many kitchens round here, so I'm trying to make my own luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say shame, I was kind of hoping it'd be bigger. At work I'd still show people the tricks I use, like getting it to scale a sauce recipe from four to forty portions. Online I'd say if it's just a tool, then the fight is still the old one: pay, rent and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I'm still a junior cook on low pay with a week's rent saved. Fratelli's is busy, so I don't think I lose the job. But I'm not getting ahead either, and that bugs me more than robots ever did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI for what it's good at and push the supper club, maybe once a month in the community hall, twelve people at twenty-five each. I'd ask the owner to put me on dough every morning so I get faster. And I'd keep pushing my mates at work to join the union, because the pay problem doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, a bit restless. Like I'd got ready for a big storm and it just drizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the supper club. Have you done one yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One, in Noor's mum's back garden, for her cousins. I used AI to plan the shopping list and the timings, and it was spot on except it forgot that our oven only fits one tray. Eight people, we made about ninety after costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supper club money go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First a proper savings pot, one month's rent, which I've never had. Then a better knife roll, because I'm still using the cheap set from the supermarket. Noor says I should also fix my bike so I stop paying for buses.

say: I'd say **shame**, I hoped AI would be bigger than a tool.
I'd say the fight is still the old one: **pay, rent and hours**.
think: Fratelli's is busy, so my **job feels safe** in this picture.
I'm **not getting ahead** on low pay, and that bugs me more than robots.
do: Run a **monthly supper club** in the community hall for twelve people.
Ask for **dough prep** every morning to get faster.
Keep pushing workmates to join the **union** over pay.
feel: **Restless**, like getting ready for a storm that only drizzled.
S0.quote: I'm not getting ahead either, and that bugs me more than robots ever did.
fieldNote: Chloe sounds almost **disappointed** that AI stays small.
Her stress is **low pay** and no savings, softened by her girlfriend's steady job.
She already treats AI as a **planning partner** for a side business.

steps.text: Run a monthly supper club for twelve guests in the community hall
Use AI to scale recipes and plan supper club shopping
Recruit Fratelli's line cooks into the hospitality union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, use it, but share the gains. At work I'd be the one showing the owner how AI can do his supplier orders. Online I'd post that if bosses save hours on paperwork, staff should get a cut, or shorter weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's more help than threat for a while. My job is hands, heat and timing, and robots are slow to come in. The owner's admin goes to software first, and that might mean he's in the kitchen more, which is fine, he's actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the ordering software at Fratelli's in the first few months, which makes me harder to let go. I'd use AI to build a proper business plan for the supper club and apply for a small start-up grant. I'd keep twenty a week aside, even if that's all I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a little uneasy for my friends in offices. Noor's sister does call centre work, and I'd worry for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said setting up the ordering makes you harder to let go. Is that a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. Fratelli's is a family business and I'm the junior, so if it ever came to cuts, I'd be first. Being the junior who knows the tech is my insurance at the pizza place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Noor's sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She answers phone calls for an energy company, all day. That's exactly the kind of job a chatbot takes. I'd help her use AI to find something else, and I'd probably feed her a lot of pasta.

say: I'd say use it, but **share the gains** with staff.
I'd post that saved paperwork hours should mean **shorter weeks** for workers.
think: My job is **hands, heat and timing**, so robots come late for me.
The owner's **admin goes first**, which might put him in the kitchen more.
do: Offer to set up **ordering software** at Fratelli's in the first months.
Use AI to write a **business plan** and apply for a start-up grant.
Keep **twenty a week** aside, however small.
feel: Mostly **excited**, a bit **uneasy** for friends in offices.
S1.quote: Being the junior who knows the tech is my insurance at the pizza place.
fieldNote: Chloe sees Steady Disruption as a **chance to be useful**, not a threat.

steps.text: Set up AI supplier ordering for the Fratelli's owner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public control, now, not after. At work I'd say let's not fight each other for the last shifts. Online I'd push for a basic income and for workers to own some of the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the thinking stuff I do on my phone gets better, which I'd enjoy. But by 2031 a robot can stretch dough faster than me, and the retail park is exactly where chains try new things first. I'd have three years before my actual job goes, and a week's rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get in first: ask the owner to let me run the robot line if he buys one, learning the maintenance and the software side. I'd go hard on the supper club in those three years, every fortnight, building a name. And I'd look at a short course in food tech or kitchen robot operating if one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and buzzing at the same time. Mostly scared about money, because Noor's pay alone doesn't cover the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a supper club look like when robots can cook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People still want a person at the table telling them about the food, I think. I'd lean into that, the story, my nan's recipes, a bit of a show. Robots can make the pasta, but I can make the night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Fratelli's doesn't want you to run the robot line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to whichever chain is installing them and ask to be trained. I'm not proud. But I'd be one of hundreds of cooks asking the same thing, which is the scary bit.

I'd push for **basic income** and workers owning some of the machines.
think: By 2031 a robot stretches **dough faster** than me, maybe at the retail park first.
I'd have **three years** and a week's rent before my job goes.

Run the **supper club fortnightly** to build a name in three years.
Look for a short **kitchen robot** operating course.

fieldNote: Chloe expects to **lose the cooking job** by 2031 but sees a way to stay useful.

steps.text: Offer to run any robot pizza line Fratelli's installs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so governments have no excuse. At work I'd tell the others to start learning the machines now. Online I'd keep pushing co-ops, kitchens owned by the people working in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five plus three is eight years before robot cooks. That's long enough for me to get properly good and get my supper club somewhere. I think I can come out of this alright if I don't waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the vocational cooking certificate at college in the first two years, because I left school early and I want something on paper. I'd move the supper club into a proper space, maybe sharing a café kitchen on Sundays. I'd use AI for the bookings, costings and social media from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Nervous about money, but I like having a race to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the certificate, if robots will cook anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when I go to a bank or a council for a grant, they want to see I'm a real chef. And I'd learn the stuff I skipped, costing and hygiene properly. Paper matters when you've got no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the supper club doesn't take off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm a qualified cook who knows AI tools, looking for a job running a robot kitchen. Not bad. Noor says I always have a plan B and never a savings account, and she's right.

I'd keep pushing **kitchen co-ops** owned by the workers.
think: Five plus three gives me **eight years** before robot cooks.
I can come out **alright** if I don't waste the time.

S3.quote: Paper matters when you've got no money.
fieldNote: Chloe uses the extra years to fix her **missing qualification**.

steps.text: Complete the vocational cooking certificate at college within two years
Rent a café kitchen on Sundays for the supper club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly and fairly. At work I'd say this is our chance to stop being the low-paid end of everything. Online I'd campaign for cheap loans so workers can buy the robots together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until the robot cooks, so I'm forty. By then I want my own little place, maybe a co-op with two or three others. Cheap robots could actually help a small kitchen like that compete with the chains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd keep cooking at Fratelli's and get faster, do the certificate, and run the supper club every month. By year five I'd want a market stall or a pop-up with a friend. Then when the robots get cheap, I'd buy one with the co-op, not be replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Hopeful even. The fast one scares me, this one feels like my kind of game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be in your co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kai from the pizza line, who's a better cook than me, and maybe Noor's cousin who does the books for a garage. Three of us, sharing the risk. I'd want it written down that we all own the same share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a week's rent saved. How does that fit a ten-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't yet, that's the honest bit. I'd have to save from the supper club every month, even fifty. Ten years of fifty is six thousand, which is a start.

I'd campaign for **cheap loans** so workers can buy robots together.
think: I want my **own little place** by forty, maybe a co-op.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years and no savings, and I'd be competing with every other cook for the few robot jobs. What would help is cheap training on the machines and a basic income so I could take a risk. Small grants for food start-ups too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd build, not just what they'd lose. I'm a junior cook with a week's rent saved, and I still want to own a kitchen one day.

headlineQuote: I'm a junior cook with a week's rent saved, and I still want to own a kitchen one day.
portrait: Chloe is a 27-year-old **junior cook** on the pasta station at a busy retail park pizzeria.
She lives with Noor, a **nursing assistant**, and has about a week's rent saved.
She uses **AI every day** and is already planning a supper club with it.
She sees slow change as a **chance**, but fast AGI as a scramble she can't fund.
Her goal is a **worker co-op** kitchen that owns its own robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with three years and no savings while competing for few robot jobs.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap machine training** and a basic income so she can take risks.
